🤖 Anthropic just made Claude Fable 5 a lot smarter about biology and a lot less frustrating to use.

One of the biggest complaints after Fable 5 launched was that it was too cautious.

Ask it to explain symptoms, help interpret lab results, or answer a biology question, and there was a good chance Claude would refuse and hand you over to the older Opus 5 model instead.

That wasn’t because Fable 5 couldn’t answer. It was because Anthropic deliberately built an extremely conservative safety system around the model. Since Fable 5 can outperform human experts on some advanced biology tasks, the company chose to err on the side of caution—even if it meant blocking thousands of perfectly harmless requests.

Now that’s changing.

Anthropic says it has redesigned the biology safety classifier, cutting biology-related fallbacks by around 85%. Instead of treating almost every biology question as potentially risky, Claude can now tell the difference between someone studying for an exam and someone asking about genuinely dangerous research.

The update means you’ll see Fable 5 much more often when asking about symptoms, lab results, biology concepts, and even clinical questions for healthcare professionals, instead of being redirected to Opus 5.

The company expects the change to reduce fallbacks by 67% on Claude AI, 55% on Cowork, 17% on Claude Code, and 7% on the Claude Platform.

The guardrails haven’t disappeared, though. Requests involving areas like virology, toxicology, molecular design, and other dual-use biological research will still trigger stricter safeguards and fall back to Opus 5.

AI just designed viruses that have never existed before… and they actually worked. 🤯

For the first time, scientists have used AI to create fully functional virus genomes from scratch, not by copying nature, but by inventing entirely new genetic designs.

Researchers from Stanford and the Arc Institute used genome language models called Evo 1 and Evo 2 to design complete genomes for Phi X174, a harmless bacteriophage that infects Escherichia coli (E. coli). To minimize biosafety risks, the models were trained only on around 2 million bacteriophage genomes, excluding viruses that infect humans, animals, or plants.

Instead of generating individual genes or proteins like previous AI systems, Evo created entire viral genomes, exploring genetic possibilities that evolution has never produced.

The researchers generated thousands of designs, synthesized 302 AI-created genomes, and tested them in the lab.

The result? 16 of them came to life.

Those AI-designed viruses successfully infected E. coli, replicated inside the bacteria, and produced new infectious offspring, proving that completely novel virus genomes designed by AI can function in the real world.

The implications are huge. This could speed up the development of phage therapies to fight antibiotic-resistant bacteria, enable custom-designed bacteriophages for medicine, and unlock entirely new tools for synthetic biology.

❗️Anthropic’s IPO problem might be Dario Amodei himself

Anthropic’s investors are reportedly getting nervous about CEO Dario Amodei’s increasingly apocalyptic messaging around AI.

One investor described him as “more of a religious leader than a CEO.”

And the stories are wild.

Dario reportedly used an offline computer to write sensitive OpenAI memos, printed documents instead of using Google Docs, avoided visiting China over kidnapping concerns, and has a reputation for ignoring outside advice.

One investor even said that before investing, they got the impression Dario “didn’t care about making money.”

Now, with Anthropic heading toward a potential IPO, some investors reportedly want him to “stop scaring everyone.”

Anthropic is trying to sell investors on the enormous economic potential of AI while its CEO is simultaneously warning the world about how dangerous that same technology could become.

Being cautious about AI risk is one thing.

But if your CEO starts sounding like he’s warning humanity about the apocalypse while you’re preparing to sell shares to the public…

investors are going to have questions. 👀

🚀 SpaceX just announced something that sounds less like a factory and more like the infrastructure for a new civilization.

In Grimes County, Texas, SpaceX plans to build Terafab, a semiconductor facility so enormous that it could become the largest chip factory ever built.

We’re talking about 100+ million square feet of manufacturing space and an initial investment of roughly $16.8 billion.

But the crazy part isn’t just the size.

Terafab is designed to bring logic, memory, advanced packaging and testing together under one roof, producing the chips needed to power Tesla’s Optimus robots, autonomous Cybercabs and SpaceX’s next generation of orbital computing.

The long-term target? 1 terawatt of compute hardware every year.

Why build a chip factory this massive? Because Tesla and SpaceX are preparing for an absurd amount of AI compute demand, potentially exceeding what today’s global semiconductor industry can supply.

So instead of waiting for the chip industry to catch up, they’re trying to build the missing capacity themselves.

Tesla builds the robots.
Tesla builds the cars.
SpaceX builds the rockets and satellites.
Terafab builds the silicon.

And then SpaceX wants to take some of that compute into orbit.

That creates an almost completely vertically integrated stack:

Silicon → AI → Robots → Cars → Rockets → Satellites → Orbital compute.

Most factories are built to serve the world as it exists today. Terafab is being designed around a world where humanity is producing machines at enormous scale, on Earth, in orbit, and eventually far beyond it.

British workers are increasingly relying on AI tools rather than lawyers to sue their employers.

Judges report that many people now use artificial intelligence to draft legal claims for employment tribunals. This shift has resulted in a significant increase in self-filed cases, as AI-generated documents remove the need for legal fees.

The employment tribunal system in Britain is under strain, with a backlog that has grown from 45,000 to 64,000 open cases within a year. Judges must still review all submitted claims, contributing to the mounting caseload.

🇺🇸 Amazon's new data center set to have America's most polluting power plant.

Amazon is backing a massive 7.65 GW natural-gas power plant in Texas to supply electricity directly to its AI data center campus.

The 35-turbine plant located 50 miles east of Pittsburgh, is permitted to emit up to 33 million tons of CO₂ annually, potentially making it the largest single permitted source of greenhouse gas emissions in the U.S.
